title: Roguelike Celebration - Lightning Talks
speaker: Thomas Robertson; Jim Shepard; Mark (surname not given); Kyla (quietdragoness); Britta; Joe Sondow
summary: A set of six 2017 lightning talks. Thomas Robertson (Artemis Spaceship Bridge Simulator) demos 'smart variables' that draw their own debug UI to speed up prototyping; Jim Shepard pitches his Stop the Hunger Clock charity trading Steam keys for local food donations; Mark shows a joke compiler from Tracery grammars to Ethereum smart contracts; Kyla reads a NetHack fanfic diary of the Oracle; Britta compares fan-fiction tropes and tags to procedural generation; and Joe Sondow shows his Star Trek parody Twitter accounts. Design content is limited to the prototyping UI idea and the fanfic-as-procedural-generation analogy.

insights.claim: Thomas Robertson's prototyping approach declares game data as 'smart variables' (with limits and lists) that can draw themselves into any given screen rectangle, removing most UI work from early prototypes.
insights.detail: Players and monsters (a flesh golem, a plant monster) are defined as data; the main loop just calls draw-my-data with a rectangle, and the UI lays itself out, including inventories and drag bars to tune values like movement speed live. It is a developer tool, not player-facing, and gets you about 80% of the way.
insights.quote: maybe these variables are smart enough to draw themselves

insights.claim: The drudgery of building UI during rapid prototyping eats time and can sap a developer's creativity and motivation to work on a game idea.
insights.detail: Robertson says you end up budgeting more time for UI whether you like it or not, leading to procrastination; this motivated his self-drawing variables experiment.
insights.quote: that drudgery is something you don't particularly like and that can actually impact your creativity

insights.claim: Jim Shepard's Stop the Hunger Clock drive gives donated Steam keys to players who buy hunger-relief food locally and mail in a receipt, deliberately avoiding a push-button online donation.
insights.detail: Developers and players donated keys. Shepard wanted people to make a difference in their own communities; one player who couldn't find food bags volunteered four hours at a church food drive instead.
insights.quote: it does not push button receive game on the internet because I want folks to go out in their community

insights.claim: Mark built a joke compiler from Tracery grammars to Ethereum smart contracts, producing permanent, unique-to-you generated text at great expense.
insights.detail: He describes it as the world's most expensive way to generate a bit of text; the default gas amount wasn't even enough to produce a string on the test chain.
insights.quote: I created a tracery to aetherium compiler so you can take your trace tracery recipe which spits out a little bit of text

insights.claim: Roguelike fan fiction exists: Kyla reads a 2015 Yuletide NetHack story written as the Oracle's diary, built around NetHack's fortune-cookie rumors and dungeon characters.
insights.detail: The Oracle receives a rumor-a-day desk calendar, takes up statue carving with Medusa's advice, throws a party, and has her statues smashed by an adventurer, ending with her ordering statue traps.
insights.quote: wrote a fanfic in nethack called just because it says readme doesn't mean you should

insights.claim: Fan fiction works like a procedural generator: writers combine tagged characters, relationship types, tropes (hurt/comfort, mirror universe) and structures ('five times X and the one time Y') into self-contained variations on familiar starting points.
insights.detail: Britta notes the tags at the top of each story act like generator inputs; she has read hundreds of stories with the same starting points and enjoys each because it's a little different, much like restarting a roguelike such as NetHack.
insights.quote: they take these structural elements that are tagged at the top of every story

insights.claim: Joe Sondow notes that Markov chain bots spun off from his hand-written Star Trek parody accounts produce a different quality of comedy than the authored originals.
insights.detail: His manual parody accounts (Picard Tips, Riker Googling, Worf Email) built the follower base that later boosted his procedural emoji bots.
insights.quote: our Markov chain BOTS that results in a different quality of comedy
